title: Cock-a-Leekie
subtitle: Scottish chicken and leek broth with prunes
excerpt: A gently flavoured Scottish soup of chicken, leeks, and rice, with prunes added in the last minutes of cooking for a sweet, slightly tart finish. Simple and restorative.

recipe.sourceNotes: Cock-a-leekie appears in Scottish records from the 16th century and is considered Scotland's oldest soup. 'Cock' refers to an old cockerel or rooster, which was the traditional bird used: an older bird that would be too tough to roast but which gave an intensely flavoured broth after long, slow cooking. The inclusion of prunes is traditional and ancient, reflecting medieval cooking conventions where sweet and savoury were not separated as they are today. Modern recipes use a whole chicken or chicken pieces rather than a cockerel. The prunes add a necessary note of sweetness that counterbalances the mild broth.

content.text: A whole chicken gives the best flavour here, producing a light, clear broth that is quite different from a stock-based soup. Skim the surface well in the first 10 minutes to keep the broth clear. The leeks go in twice: the first batch cooks with the chicken and gives flavour to the broth; a second batch is added near the end for texture. The prunes are added in the last 10 minutes so they soften but do not disintegrate.

Place the chicken in a large pot. Cover with 2 litres of cold water. Bring to a boil. Skim well. Add half the leeks, the bay leaves, thyme, peppercorns, and 1 teaspoon of salt. Simmer gently for 1 hour until the chicken is cooked through.
Lift the chicken out. Strain the broth through a fine sieve, discarding the spent vegetables and aromatics. Return the clear broth to the pan. Add the rice and remaining leeks. Simmer for 15 minutes.

While the rice cooks, strip the chicken meat from the carcass, discarding the skin and bones. Shred the meat. Add the chicken and prunes to the broth. Simmer for 10 minutes. Season with the remaining salt. Stir in the parsley and serve.
